value.overview: The Hudsonian Godwit (Limosa haemastica) is a long-distance migrating shorebird of the sandpiper family. It breeds in subarctic tundra and wetlands of Alaska and northern Canada, then travels to southern South America for the nonbreeding season. Its migration route spans much of the Americas, and some individuals pass through Central America. In Costa Rica, it is an uncommon to rare migrant found mainly at suitable coastal wetlands and mudflats.
value.classification: The Hudsonian Godwit belongs to the sandpiper family, Scolopacidae, in the order Charadriiformes. It is one of four living godwit species in the genus Limosa.
value.identification: This is a medium-large shorebird with a long, slightly upturned, two-colored bill, long gray legs, and a white eyebrow. Breeding adults are richly rufous below with dark, mottled upperparts, while nonbreeding birds are mostly gray above and pale below. In flight, the white rump and wing stripe contrast with dark underwings and a dark tail. It is smaller and generally darker than the Marbled Godwit, with a shorter, more upturned bill.
value.rangeHabitat: Hudsonian Godwits breed in grassy tundra, sedge meadows, bogs, and wet areas near ponds in Alaska and northern Canada. During migration and winter they use tidal mudflats, estuaries, salt marshes, freshwater wetlands, shallow pools, beaches, rice fields, and other open wet habitats. Costa Rica lies outside the breeding and wintering ranges. The species occurs there mainly as an uncommon or rare passage migrant, especially at coastal mudflats, estuaries, salt ponds, and other shorebird habitats.
value.migrationStatus: A long-distance migrant. Birds move between subarctic breeding grounds and southern South America. In Costa Rica, it is a scarce and irregular migrant, with records most likely during northbound and southbound passage rather than as a regular resident.
value.breeding: Breeding occurs in the subarctic, primarily across northern Canada and Alaska. Pairs nest on the ground in tundra or wet meadow habitats, often near shallow ponds and scattered shrubs or trees. The female usually lays a small clutch in a shallow depression lined with vegetation. Both adults participate in incubation and care of the young. Hudsonian Godwits have a short breeding season and must time nesting closely with the brief northern summer.
value.dietFeeding: The species feeds mainly on insects and other invertebrates during the breeding season, including beetles, flies, larvae, worms, and other small prey. During migration and winter it takes marine worms, mollusks, crustaceans, insects, and sometimes small fish or plant material. It commonly probes soft mud with its bill, walks through shallow water, and searches wet fields and marshes for exposed prey.
value.behavior: Hudsonian Godwits are social outside the breeding season and often gather in flocks with other large shorebirds such as Willets, yellowlegs, and other godwits. They make powerful, direct flights and may travel very long distances between stopover sites. At feeding areas they walk steadily while probing the substrate. Flocks roost on islands, beaches, exposed mud, floating vegetation, or open grassy areas, and they can be sensitive to repeated human disturbance.

conservation.populationTrend: Generally considered stable globally, with possible declines in some populations or regions. Monitoring remains difficult because the species is widely dispersed during migration and breeding.
